div.p: Geographically weighted regression model with a spatially autoregressive term of the response variable (GWR-Lag model for short) is a useful tool to simultaneously model spatial autocorrelation in the response variable and spatial heterogeneity in the regression relationship. The profile maximum likelihood estimation has been developed to calibrate the model, where a single bandwidth is used for all of the spatially varying coefficients. However, due to different spatial scales at which the explanatory variables might operate, the coefficients may have different levels of spatial heterogeneity and cannot be effectively estimated by a single bandwidth. To deal with such multiscale problem, a backfitting method is proposed to calibrate the GWR-Lag model, where the optimal bandwidth size is separately selected for each coefficient and the autoregressive parameter is estimated by maximizing the log-likelihood function. A simulation study with a comparison of the GWR-based profile maximum likelihood (GWR-ML) estimation is conducted to assess the performance of the backfitting approach. The empirical results show that the backfitting method not only provides useful scale information for each explanatory variable, but also yields more accurate estimators of the coefficients. Furthermore, a real-life data set is analyzed to demonstrate the effectiveness of the backfitting approach.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity are two fundamental properties of spatial data that may appear simultaneously in the real world (Can 1992;Patton and McErlean 2003). Fotheringham (2009) and Pace and LeSage (2004a) pointed out that spatial autocorrelation may evoke spatial heterogeneity and vice versa. Geniaux and Martinetti (2018) argued that spatial heterogeneity in regression models is inseparable from spatial autocorrelation. Therefore, it is necessary to simultaneously consider these two properties in spatial regression models.

In spatial econometrics, two kinds of spatial autocorrelation are commonly considered in a linear regression model. One is spatial autocorrelation in the response variable and the other is spatial autocorrelation in the error term, corresponding to spatial autoregressive (SAR) models and spatial error models (SEM), respectively. As explained in a number of research in the literature (e.g., Case 1991;Anselin and Bera 1998;Kim, Phipps, and Anselin 2003;Kelejian, Tavlas, and Hondroyiannis 2006;LeSage and Pace 2009), by incorporating spatial autocorrelation in the response variable into the model, SAR models not only capture the direct impacts from changes in the explanatory variables, but can also derive the indirect impacts (or spillover effects) that are eliminated in SEM. Therefore, much attention has been paid to the study and application of SAR models (see, e.g., Case 1991;Case, Rosen, and Hines 1993;Murdoch, Sandler, and Sargent 1997;Brueckner 1998;Fingleton 2000;LeSage and Pace 2009;Sparks and Sparks 2010;Gebremariam, Gebremedhin, and Schaeffer 2012;Liu et al. 2018;Zou, Zhan, and Zhang 2018). Nevertheless, as pointed out by Geniaux and Martinetti (2018), only taking into account spatial autocorrelation could not handle the issue related to spatial heterogeneity which may be caused by the misspecification of spatial autocorrelation. In addition, unobserved explanatory variables that are correlated to the observed ones can also lead to spatial heterogeneity in the regression relationship (Fotheringham, Brunsdon, and Charlton 2002). Therefore, it is crucial to further consider spatial heterogeneity in the regression models with spatial autocorrelation.

Spatial heterogeneity has received much attention in geo-referenced data analysis. The wellknown models in exploring spatial heterogeneity of a regression relationship are the geographically weighted regression (GWR) models (Brunsdon, Fotheringham, and Charlton 1996), in which the regression coefficients are assumed to be the functions of spatial coordinates. Since the inception of the GWR models, there has been a substantial study on their statistical inferences and applications (see, e.g., Brunsdon, Fotheringham, and Charlton 1999;Leung, Mei, and Zhang 2000;Fotheringham, Brunsdon, and Charlton 2002;Huang and Leung 2002;Páez, Uchida, and Miyamoto 2002;Wheeler 2009;Lu et al. 2014;Mei, Xu, and Wang 2016;Kim, Tanaka, and Ge 2018;Wang et al. 2018). However, a flaw of the GWR model is that it ignores spatial autocorrelation (Pace and LeSage 2004a) because of the assumption of independent model errors. Recently, Li, Mei, and Wang (2019) have empirically demonstrated that, in certain cases, ignoring spatial autocorrelation in the response variable may lead to biased or even invalid estimators of the regression coefficients in a GWR model when spatial autocorrelation does exist in the response variable.

Therefore, it is promising to introduce the spatial autocorrelation into the traditional GWR model to simultaneously account for both spatial heterogeneity and spatial autocorrelation. In a class of such models summarized in Geniaux and Martinetti (2018), the GWR model with a spatial lag term of the response variable, called GWR-Lag model in short henceforth, is perhaps one of the most important models in view of the advantages of both SAR and GWR models. In regard to the calibration of the GWR-Lag models, Brunsdon, Fotheringham, and Charlton (1998) proposed an approach by combining the GWR and the profile maximum likelihood-based methods; and Sun et al. (2014) formulated a local-linear profile maximum likelihood estimation procedure and derived the asymptotic properties of the related estimators. In addition, Geniaux and Martinetti (2018) suggested the use of a spatial two-stage least square to calibrate the models. For statistical inferences of the GWR-Lag models, Li, Mei, and Wang (2019) proposed bootstrap procedures to test whether the spatial lag term exists and whether some coefficients are constant; Sun et al. (2014) used the AIC or BIC criterion for identifying possible constant coefficients. In particular, the bootstrap test for the existence of spatial autocorrelation in the response variable derived by Li, Mei, and Wang (2019) can be used to select an appropriate model between a GWR-Lag model and a GWR model for a given data set. However, in these existing estimation and inference methods, all of the spatially varying coefficients in the GWR-Lag models are calibrated by a single bandwidth, which does not take into account the influence of spatial scale at which each explanatory variable operates.

Scale is a fundamental geographic concept and it has been recognized that different spatial processes generally operate at different spatial scales (Fotheringham, Yang, and Kang 2017). In the GWR-related models, each regression coefficient is inherently subjected to the effect of a scale at which the corresponding explanatory variable operates and will possibly show a different level of spatial heterogeneity. As well documented in the statistical varying coefficient models with nonparametric kernel smoothing estimation, a coefficient with a higher level of heterogeneity requires a smaller bandwidth size and a lower level of heterogeneity calls for a larger bandwidth size (Fan and Zhang 1999), which means that different bandwidths should be used for different explanatory variables. The backfitting technique (Hastie and Tibshirani 1986) can well achieve the task of separately selecting bandwidth size for each regression coefficient. In addition, the scale in the geographical space may also cause the variation of the bandwidths especially when the sampling points (or regions) are not equally distributed over space, which has aroused an interest in using adaptive bandwidths (Gollini et al. 2013). Recently, the backfitting technique has been successfully applied to the GWR models for dealing with the multiscale issue (Fotheringham, Yang, and Kang 2017;Leong and Yue 2017). This multiscale calibration method not only provides the scale information on each explanatory variable via the separately selected optimal bandwidth sizes, but also yields more efficient estimators of the spatially varying coefficients. In this article, we combine the backfitting procedure with the profile maximum likelihood estimation method to calibrate the GWR-Lag models. Specifically, the backfitting procedure is used to calibrate the spatially varying coefficients for handling the multiscale issue among the explanatory variables, and the profile maximum likelihood method is employed to estimate the autoregressive parameter in the spatial lag term. In this way, we expect that not only the scales at which the explanatory variables operate can be uncovered via the separately selected optimal bandwidth sizes for the coefficients, but the efficient estimators for both the autoregressive parameter and the spatially varying coefficients can also be obtained.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. In Section 2, the backfitting estimation of the GWR models and the profile maximum likelihood estimation of the GWR-Lag models are briefly introduced. In Section 3, the backfitting procedure for calibrating the GWR-Lag models is formulated in detail. In Section 4, a simulation experiment with some measurement indices is designed to evaluate the performance of the proposed backfitting estimation approach, followed by the analysis of the simulation results in Section 5. A real-world example based on the Boston housing price data are given in Section 6 to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed backfitting method of the GWR-Lag models. The article is then concluded with final remarks including a summary and discussions on the computability of the backfitting method and possible directions for further research.

div.head: Simulation study
div.p: In order to assess the performance of the backfitting method on tackling the multiscale problem and estimating the coefficients, a simulation experiment with a comparison of the GWR-ML estimation is designed. Moreover, an additional model is built to examine the impact of ignoring an explanatory variable that is correlated with some explanatory variables in the model on the estimators of the coefficients.

div.head: The spatial layout
div.p: In the simulation, we used a unit square to represent the spatial region with its bottom-left corner being the origin of the Cartesian coordinate system. In view of the fact that the sampling locations in most of the practical problems are irregularly distributed, the sampling locations were determined by independently drawing a pair of random numbers from the uniform distribution U(0, 1).

div.p: The kernel weights with an adaptive bandwidth have been reckoned to be a favorable way for dealing with data collected at irregular locations (Gollini et al. 2013). div.head: Simulation results and interpretations
div.p: The result with analysis for Model 1 The average value, absolute bias, standard deviation, and root mean square error for estimating the autoregressive parameter ρ in N = 500 replications are reported in Table 1, from which we can observe that the performance of the backfitting method is nearly the same as that of the GWR-ML method and both methods yield very accurate estimators of ρ in all of the experiment settings. Furthermore, the estimation accuracy from both methods is improved with the increase of the sample size in terms of the root mean square error.

To evaluate the ability of the backfitting method in uncovering the different scales at which the explanatory variables operate, the boxplots of the selected optimal bandwidth sizes of h in the 500 replications for n = 400 are depicted in Fig. 2, in which h * denotes the optimal sizes of h selected in the GWR-ML method, and h * 1 , h * 2 , and h * 3 represent the optimal bandwidth sizes of β 1 (u, v), β 2 (u, v), and β 3 (u, v) determined in the backfitting approach. The boxplots for n = 600 are essentially the same as those for n = 400, which we therefore omitted here. For each value of ρ, Fig. 2 shows that β 1 (u, v) has the smallest optimal bandwidth size followed by β 2 (u, v), and β 3 (u, v) has the largest optimal bandwidth size, which is in line with the levels of spatial heterogeneity of the three regression coefficients shown in Fig. 1. This result is also consistent with the common finding that a coefficient with a higher level of spatial heterogeneity needs a smaller bandwidth size while a lower level of spatial heterogeneity requires a larger bandwidth size. Furthermore, the optimal bandwidth sizes for each coefficient in the 500 replications are very stable. The boxplots indicate that the backfitting method has the promising ability in determining an appropriate bandwidth size for each of the regression coefficients in the GWR-Lag model. It is shown that the MAbias and MRMSE values of the backfitting estimators for the three coefficients are consistently smaller than those of the GWR-ML estimators, indicating that the backfitting method yields more accurate coefficient estimators. The most notable improvement in the estimation accuracy is observed in β 3 (u, v). The reason may be that β 3 (u, v) is spatially stationary and needs a large bandwidth size to be calibrated. However, the bandwidth size selected in the GWR-ML method is much smaller, leading to a poor estimator of β 3 (u, v). In contrast, the backfitting method can result in an appropriate bandwidth size for each coefficient and produce more accurate coefficient estimators accordingly. Furthermore, it is observed from Table 2 that the performance of both methods in estimating the spatially varying coefficients is improved with the increase of the sample size. In addition, to visually understand the absolute biases of the coefficient estimators at each location, the heatmaps of with n = 400 and ρ = 0 are depicted in Fig. 3. The maps clearly show that larger absolute biases usually appear at the border region and the neighborhoods of the locations where the coefficients reach their respective maximal or minimal values, and the absolute biases of the backfitting estimators are generally smaller than those of the GWR-ML estimators especially for the estimator of β 3 (u, v). In particular, the estimation accuracy of the coefficient of X 1 that is correlated to the ignored variable X 2 is evidently reduced, which implies that the unobserved variable can change the underlying spatial heterogeneity of the coefficient of X 1 . Furthermore, the estimation accuracy of the autoregressive parameter ρ and the intercept β 0 (u, v) becomes even worse in the cases of strong spatial autocorrelation. The reason is perhaps that the effect of the unobserved variable with a different scale will end up in the other terms, especially the intercept and the coefficient of the explanatory variable that is correlated with the unobserved one, leading to inaccurate estimators of ρ and the spatially varying coefficients in the model. On the whole, however, the backfitting method still yields more accurate estimators for both ρ and the coefficients in terms of the defined indices. The boxplots of the optimal bandwidth sizes in the 500 replications for each value of ρ are depicted in Fig. 4, which illustrates that the backfitting estimation still yields appropriate bandwidth sizes for the coefficients with different levels of spatial heterogeneity, and the uncertainty of the optimal bandwidth sizes of β 3 (u, v) in Model 2 is obviously reduced compared to the optimal bandwidth sizes of β 3 (u, v) in Fig. 2.

div.head: A real-life application
div.p: In this section, the proposed backfitting estimation is applied to the well-known Boston housing price data set given in Hurrison and Rubinfeld (1978) and corrected for a few minor errors by Gilley and Pace (1996). The data set consists of the median value (MEDV in $1,000) of owner-occupied homes and 13 explanatory variables in 506 U.S. census tracts in 1970, and is available in the R package spdep (http://cran.r-proje ct.org/). Since the focus of this example is to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed backfitting calibration method, only the following explanatory variables are considered here:

• CRIM: per capita crime rate by town; • RM: average number of rooms in owner-occupied homes per dwelling; • DIS: weighted distances to five Boston employment centers; • PTRATIO: pupil-teacher ration by town school district; • LSTAT: proportion of the lower status population.

Through fitting a GWR-Lag model by the GWR-LM method, the statistical test developed by Li, Mei, and Wang (2019) has demonstrated that there exists significant autocorrelation among the observations of MEDV, although more explanatory variables were used in that article. Based on this finding, we then consider the following GWR-Lag model:

where the spatial weight matrix W = (w ij ) n×n was formulated in the binary way according to the given neighbor list of each census tract. The backfitting and GWR-ML methods were employed to calibrate this model, in which the explanatory variables were centralized, the Epanechnikov kernel function with an adaptive bandwidth was used to generate the kernel weights, the optimal bandwidth size was selected by the AICc criterion, and the convergence threshold in the backfitting procedure was set to be η 0 = 0.01. In addition, for the purpose of comparison, the corresponding GWR and SAR models were also fitted by the traditional GWR method and the maximum likelihood estimation, respectively.

The estimators of ρ from the backfitting method, the GWR-ML method and the SAR model are 0.645, 0.345, and 0.500, respectively, indicating that there exists spatial autocorrelation among the housing prices, but the intensity varies among the models considered and the estimation methods used. It should be noted that only a part of the explanatory variables in the data set enter into various models. According to the foregoing simulation result, the estimator of ρ from each model or calibration method may be affected by the unused explanatory variables, but that estimated by the backfitting method of the GWR-Lag model may be more accurate. The optimal bandwidth sizes selected in the GWR-ML method and the GWR model are both 85, while those selected for β 0 (u, v), β 1 (u, v), β 2 (u, v), β 3 (u, v), β 4 (u, v), and β 5 (u, v) in the backfitting estimation are 21, 506, 21, 66, 506, and 506, respectively. The optimal bandwidth sizes from the backfitting estimation provide the information about the different scales at which the explanatory variables operate, on which we may infer that the coefficients β 0 (u, v), β 2 (u, v), and β 3 (u, v) are spatially varying while the coefficients β 1 (u, v), β 4 (u, v), and β 5 (u, v) may be thought to be constant since their optimal bandwidth sizes are equal to the sample size. In addition, the residual sums of squares for the GWR-Lag model with the backfitting and GWR-ML methods, the GWR model and the SAR model are 4747.6, 5098.6, 6260.7, and 8347.1, respectively, showing that the GWR-Lag model with the backfitting estimation yields the best fit.

The heatmaps of the estimators of the coefficients β 0 (u, v), β 2 (u, v), and β 3 (u, v) from the GWR-Lag model with the backfitting and GWR-ML estimation methods and the corresponding GWR model are shown in Fig. 5, and those of β 1 (u, v), β 4 (u, v), and β 5 (u, v) are depicted in Fig. 6. The coefficient estimators by the backfitting method exhibit distinct patterns that the coefficients β 1 (u, v), β 4 (u, v), and β 5 (u, v) seem to be constant and the others are spatially varying. Combining the findings in the simulation and the above results of the optimal bandwidth sizes and the values of residual sum of squares, we may conclude that the coefficient estimators obtained by the backfitting method are more convincible. In view of the impact of the explanatory variable, the average number of rooms in owneroccupied homes per dwelling (RM) positively influences the housing price in most areas with the intensity increasing from the central part to the peripheral parts; the weighted distances to five Boston employment centers (DIS) negatively affects the housing price with the intensity decreasing from the central part to the peripheral parts; the per capita crime rate by town (CRIM), the pupil-teacher ration by town school district (PTRATIO), and the proportion of the lower status population (LSTAT) have approximately global negative influence on the housing price.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this article, a backfitting estimation method is proposed to deal with the multiscale issue in the GWR-Lag models in which spatial autocorrelation in the response variable and spatial (a) (b)

heterogeneity in the regression relationship are simultaneously considered. The simulation study demonstrates that the backfitting approach not only provides the information on the spatial scale at which each explanatory variable operates for a better understanding of the underlying spatial process, but also improves the estimation accuracy of the regression coefficients when they have different levels of spatial heterogeneity. Moreover, the simulation study also shows that the backfitting method can alleviate the influence of unobservable explanatory variables that are correlated to those in the model and yield more accurate estimators of both the autoregressive parameter and the spatially varying coefficients compared to the GWR-ML estimation method.

In regard to the computability issue of the proposed backfitting estimation for the GWR-Lag models, the main computation cost comes from two parts. The first part is the iterative calibration of as many GWR models as there are spatially varying coefficients, in which the selection of the optimal bandwidth size for each GWR model is time consuming. The second part is the use of the maximum likelihood (ML) approach to estimate the autoregressive parameter ρ, in which the computation of the determinant of I n -ρW or the eigenvalues of W is extremely expensive compared to the spatial two-stage least square (2SLS) method in Geniaux and Martinetti (2018), although the ML approach has the advantage of a better behavior of the estimator for high values of ρ. The simulation study conducted in Section 4 demonstrates that the computational efficiency of the proposed backfitting method is acceptable for a small or moderate sample size. However, the computation time will exponentially increase with the increase of the sample size and the number of the explanatory variables. Therefore, there is a need for an improvement of the computability of the proposed method in order to make it applicable and efficient to the analysis of big data. The recently developed algorithms such as the parallelization or the use of a sparse matrix for calibrating the GWR-typed models (Li et al. 2019;Li and Fotheringham 2020) have great potential in improving the computational efficiency in the first part. The algorithms for efficiently calculating the determinants or the eigenvalues of large sparse matrices (Pace and LeSage 2004b;Aktulga et al. 2014) could be used in the second part in view of the fact that the spatial adjacency matrix W is in general sparse in most of the real-world problems. Nevertheless, details of the plausible use of these algorithms in the proposed backfitting estimation of the GWR-Lag models remain to be investigated.

The main focus of the proposed backfitting method is on the different levels of spatial heterogeneity in the regression coefficients. Like the work of the hyper GWR in Comber et al. (2018), if we further allow the bandwidth of each explanatory variable to vary with location, more accurate estimators of the coefficients could be obtained, which undoubtedly amounts to a huge computation cost. However, based on the development of the big data-oriented algorithms for the multiscale GWR-Lag models, it is possible to successfully achieve the task.

It is also an interesting topic to further identify possible constant coefficients in a GWR-Lag model based on the proposed backfitting method. Although the separately selected bandwidth size for each regression coefficient can provide the information for us to judge the level of spatial heterogeneity of each coefficient, formal tests need to be developed to give the inference a solid statistical basis. In addition, the local standard errors of the estimators of each coefficient are an important measure to reflect the local variation of the estimators and to further formulate a formal local statistical significance test for the influence of each explanatory variable on the response variable at each location. For further research, it is worthwhile to investigate the plausible extension of the way for deriving the hat matrix in the multiscale GWR in Yu et al. (2020) in order to achieve the task of solving the local standard errors for the backfitting estimators of the coefficients in the GWR-Lag models.
